```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
# load your data here and any pre-processing/cleaning 
# Load data set
student_math <- read_rds("data/student_math.rds")

# Remove unnecessary columns and missing mathematics scores
student_math_pro <- student_math |>
  select(-general_family_support) |>
  filter(
    if_all(
      starts_with("math_score_pv"),
      ~ !is.na(.)
    )
  )

# Select variables for the investigation
student_processed <- student_math_pro |>
  select(
    student_id,
    country_code,
    student_age,
    student_gender,
    family_socioeconomic_status,
    family_support,
    home_possessions_index,
    home_ict_resources,
    highest_parental_education,
    parental_education_years,
    highest_parental_occupational_status,
    starts_with("math_score_pv")
  )

# Calculate mean mathematics score
student_processed <- student_processed |>
  mutate(
    math_score = rowMeans(
      across(starts_with("math_score_pv"))
    )
  ) |>
  select(-starts_with("math_score_pv"))


```


## Research Question

Describe your research question here. Include why this question might be of interest. 

**Question**: 
*How are parental education, parental occupational status, and home ICT resources associated with students’ mathematics performance in PISA 2025?*

**Why**:
*Students' home environments may play an important role in their educational outcomes. Differences in parental education, occupational status, and access to ICT resources may be associated with students' opportunities to learn and their mathematics performance. Investigating these relationships can help us better understand how family background relates to educational achievement.*

### Dataset overview

*This investigation uses student-level data from the PISA 2025 Student Questionnaire, published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). The dataset contains information on students' backgrounds and mathematics performance, allowing us to investigate the associations between family circumstances and academic achievement (OECD, n.d.).*

### Key variables

Our investigation focuses on three main factors that may be related to students' mathematics performance.

Mathematics performance: math_score represents each student's mathematics performance.

Parental education: We use parental_education_years to show the number of years of education completed by parents. We also kept highest_parental_education in the dataset.

Parental occupational status: We use highest_parental_occupational_status to examine whether parents' occupational status is related to students' mathematics performance.

Home ICT resources: We use home_ict_resources to represent the ICT resources available at home.

Other variables, such as student age, gender, country, family socioeconomic status and home possessions, were also kept to provide more information about students' backgrounds.

### Data processing

Our starting material came in two parts: the PISA 2025 data file and the student questionnaire. We worked from the data file only, so the questionnaire was set aside and everything below is based on the 755,721 student rows in `student_math`.

We first used `summary()` in R to check the data and identify missing values. Mathematics scores were missing for two countries, so we excluded them: Uzbekistan (all of its records) and Belgium (one record). That took out 8,653 records, leaving 747,068 students.

To make the data easier to use, we calculated the average of the ten mathematics scores for each student using `rowMeans()`. We created a new variable called `math_score` and then removed the original ten score columns.

We then selected the variables needed for our research: mathematics scores, parental education, parental occupational status and home ICT resources.

We did not remove all missing values from the other variables at this stage. Instead, we excluded missing observations when needed for individual visualisations and analyses, so that each analysis kept as many students as its own variables allowed, rather than losing rows it did not use.

The table sets the processed data against the original file: `student_math` (755,721 rows, 24 variables) and `student_processed` (747,068 rows, 12 variables, after irrelevant variables were dropped and the ten plausible values became one `math_score`).

### Data citation
The dataset was retrieved on 28 October 2026 from the OECD PISA 2025 database: https://webfs.oecd.org/pisa2022/index.html.
